scenarios.scenarioText: Nexgen Technologies Ltd. (NTL) is a listed company on BSE and NSE with a market capitalisation of Rs. 8,200 crore, consolidated annual turnover of Rs. 3,400 crore, and 42,000 shareholders. The board of NTL comprises 12 directors: (i) Mr. Ashwin Mehta — Executive Chairman and Promoter (holding 34.2% equity); (ii) Mr. Vivek Saxena — Managing Director; (iii) Mr. Rohan Gupta — Whole-Time Director (Operations); (iv) Ms. Kavita Iyer — Whole-Time Director (Finance) who also serves as the CFO; (v) Mr. Suresh Nair — Non-Executive Non-Independent Director (nominee of LIC, holding 8.1%); (vi) Mr. Prakash Jain — Non-Executive Non-Independent Director (Promoter Group); (vii) Ms. Ananya Deshmukh — Independent Director (appointed January 2021, first term of 5 years); (viii) Dr. Rajan Pillai — Independent Director (appointed March 2016, completed first term of 5 years in March 2021, reappointed for second term ending March 2026); (ix) Ms. Fatima Sheikh — Independent Director (appointed April 2023); (x) Mr. David Thomas — Independent Director (appointed June 2024); (xi) Ms. Priya Sharma — Independent Director (appointed September 2025); and (xii) Mr. Karthik Reddy — Independent Director (appointed November 2025). The company's last four board meetings were held on: January 15, 2026; April 28, 2026; September 2, 2026; and December 18, 2026. NTL's Nomination and Remuneration Committee (NRC) consists of Mr. Suresh Nair (Chairman), Ms. Ananya Deshmukh, and Mr. Vivek Saxena (MD). The Audit Committee consists of Dr. Rajan Pillai (Chairman), Ms. Fatima Sheikh, Mr. Prakash Jain, and Ms. Kavita Iyer (WTD-Finance/CFO). The company is now preparing for Dr. Pillai's retirement at the end of his second term in March 2026 and needs to reconstitute both committees.

questions.question: NTL's board has 12 directors, of whom 4 are executive directors (Mr. Mehta as Executive Chairman, Mr. Saxena as MD, Mr. Gupta as WTD, and Ms. Iyer as WTD/CFO). Given that the chairperson is an executive promoter director, which of the following CORRECTLY evaluates whether NTL's board composition complies with Regulation 17 of SEBI LODR?

options.A: NTL needs at least 6 independent directors (50% of board strength) since the chairperson is executive, and with 6 IDs currently on the board (Ms. Deshmukh, Dr. Pillai, Ms. Sheikh, Mr. Thomas, Ms. Sharma, Mr. Reddy), the requirement is exactly met
options.B: NTL needs at least 4 independent directors (one-third of board strength) since the requirement of half the board being IDs applies only when the chairperson is a non-executive promoter, not an executive promoter chairman
options.C: NTL needs at least 6 non-executive directors (50% of board strength) as per Regulation 17, and the independent director requirement is separately one-third regardless of whether the chairman is executive or non-executive
options.D: NTL needs at least 8 independent directors since Regulation 17 requires two-thirds of the board to be IDs when the chairperson is both executive AND a promoter, which is a stricter standard than just an executive chairperson

questions.explanation: Under Regulation 17(1)(b) of SEBI LODR, where the chairperson of the board is an executive director (which Mr. Ashwin Mehta is — he is the Executive Chairman), at least HALF of the board shall comprise independent directors. With a 12-member board, this means at least 6 IDs are required. NTL currently has 6 IDs (Ms. Deshmukh, Dr. Pillai, Ms. Sheikh, Mr. Thomas, Ms. Sharma, Mr. Reddy), so the requirement is exactly met. Option B is the most dangerous trap — it states 'one-third' which is the requirement when the chairperson is NON-EXECUTIVE (Regulation 17(1)(a)). Students who confuse the two thresholds will pick this. The key distinction: non-executive chairperson → 1/3 IDs; executive chairperson → 1/2 IDs. Option C confuses 'non-executive' with 'independent' — the regulation specifically requires independent directors, not merely non-executive directors. Option D fabricates a 'two-thirds' requirement that does not exist anywhere in LODR. The scenario fact that Mr. Mehta is BOTH executive AND promoter is a red herring — the trigger for the higher threshold is being executive, not being a promoter.

questions.question: NTL held board meetings on January 15, April 28, September 2, and December 18, 2026. Regarding the frequency and gap requirements under Regulation 17(2) of SEBI LODR, which of the following is CORRECT?

options.A: NTL has complied with Regulation 17(2) because it held 4 meetings in the calendar year with no gap exceeding 120 days between consecutive meetings
options.B: NTL has violated Regulation 17(2) because the gap between the April 28 meeting and the September 2 meeting is 127 days, which exceeds the maximum permitted gap of 120 days between two consecutive board meetings
options.C: NTL has violated Regulation 17(2) because it held only 4 meetings when listed companies are required to hold a minimum of 6 board meetings per financial year under LODR
options.D: NTL has complied because the 120-day gap rule applies only between the last meeting of one financial year and the first meeting of the next financial year, not between consecutive meetings within the same year

questions.explanation: Under Regulation 17(2) of SEBI LODR, the board shall meet at least 4 times a year with a maximum gap of 120 days between any two consecutive meetings. Calculating the gaps: Jan 15 to Apr 28 = 103 days (OK); Apr 28 to Sep 2 = 127 days (EXCEEDS 120 days — VIOLATION); Sep 2 to Dec 18 = 107 days (OK). The gap of 127 days between the April 28 and September 2 meetings violates the 120-day maximum. Option A is the trap for students who count only the number of meetings (4) without computing the actual gaps. Meeting the minimum number alone is insufficient — the gap requirement must also be satisfied. Option C fabricates a '6 meetings' requirement — the minimum is 4 per year under LODR (students may confuse this with some other provision). Option D incorrectly limits the 120-day gap rule to inter-year gaps only — it applies between ANY two consecutive board meetings. The scenario deliberately places the meetings with a gap slightly exceeding 120 days (127 days) to test whether students actually compute the gaps rather than just counting meetings.

questions.question: NTL's Nomination and Remuneration Committee (NRC) consists of Mr. Suresh Nair (Non-Executive Non-Independent, Chairman), Ms. Ananya Deshmukh (ID), and Mr. Vivek Saxena (MD). Regarding the composition of the NRC under Regulation 19 of SEBI LODR, which of the following statements about violations is CORRECT?

options.A: The NRC composition has only one violation: Mr. Vivek Saxena (MD) cannot be a member because all NRC members must be non-executive directors; the chairmanship of Mr. Suresh Nair (non-executive) is permissible since LODR does not require the NRC chairman to be independent
options.B: The NRC composition has two violations: (i) Mr. Vivek Saxena (MD) is an executive director and cannot be a member, and (ii) Mr. Suresh Nair cannot be the chairman because the chairperson of the NRC must be an independent director under Regulation 19
options.C: The NRC composition is fully compliant because Regulation 19 requires at least one independent director on the NRC, Ms. Deshmukh satisfies this, and the MD is permitted as a member to provide management perspective
options.D: The NRC composition has three violations: (i) Saxena is executive, (ii) Nair is not independent, and (iii) the committee must have at least 4 members for companies with market capitalisation exceeding Rs. 5,000 crore

questions.explanation: Under Regulation 19(1) of SEBI LODR, the NRC shall comprise at least 3 directors, ALL of whom must be NON-EXECUTIVE directors, with not less than HALF being independent directors, and the chairperson of the NRC must be an INDEPENDENT director. Violation 1: Mr. Vivek Saxena (MD) is an executive director and cannot be a member — all members must be non-executive. Violation 2: Mr. Suresh Nair is the chairman but he is non-executive NON-INDEPENDENT — the chairman must be an independent director. Also, with only 1 ID out of 3 members (Ms. Deshmukh), the 'majority IDs' requirement is not met. Option A correctly identifies Violation 1 but incorrectly states that a non-executive non-independent chairman is permissible — Regulation 19(2) specifically requires the NRC chairperson to be an ID. This is the 'close but not quite' trap. Option C is completely wrong — it understates the requirements (just 'one ID' instead of 'majority IDs'). Option D adds a fabricated 4-member minimum based on market cap that doesn't exist. The key scenario facts are the specific roles: Saxena is MD (executive), Nair is LIC nominee (non-executive non-independent).

questions.question: NTL's Audit Committee consists of Dr. Rajan Pillai (ID, Chairman), Ms. Fatima Sheikh (ID), Mr. Prakash Jain (Non-Executive Non-Independent), and Ms. Kavita Iyer (WTD-Finance/CFO). Which of the following CORRECTLY identifies ALL compliance issues with this Audit Committee composition under Regulation 18 of SEBI LODR?

options.A: Only one violation: Ms. Kavita Iyer (WTD/CFO) cannot be a member because all Audit Committee members must be non-executive directors; the rest of the composition is compliant
options.B: Two violations: (i) Ms. Kavita Iyer (WTD) cannot be a member as only non-executive directors can be members, and (ii) Mr. Prakash Jain, being a promoter group non-executive non-independent director, is disqualified from the Audit Committee
options.C: No violations: Regulation 18 permits the CFO to be a member of the Audit Committee as a permanent invitee with no voting rights, and there is no bar on non-executive non-independent directors being members, provided IDs form the majority
options.D: Three violations: (i) Ms. Iyer is executive, (ii) the committee must have minimum 4 non-executive members, and (iii) the CFO cannot even attend Audit Committee meetings to avoid conflict of interest

questions.explanation: Under Regulation 18(1) of SEBI LODR, the Audit Committee shall have minimum 3 directors as members, and two-thirds of the members shall be independent directors. ALL members must be non-executive directors, with the chairperson being an independent director. The only violation here is that Ms. Kavita Iyer (WTD-Finance/CFO) is an executive director and cannot be a MEMBER of the Audit Committee. The remaining composition — Dr. Pillai (ID, Chairman), Ms. Sheikh (ID), and Mr. Jain (Non-Executive Non-Independent) — is permissible. With Pillai and Sheikh as IDs out of 3 remaining non-executive members, IDs would form 2/3 majority, satisfying the requirement. Option B incorrectly disqualifies Mr. Prakash Jain — there is no bar on promoter group non-executive non-independent directors being Audit Committee members, provided IDs form two-thirds of the membership. Option C wrongly states the CFO can be a 'permanent invitee' member — the CFO may be invited to attend meetings but cannot be a MEMBER. Option D fabricates requirements. Note: the CFO and auditors typically attend Audit Committee meetings as invitees, not as members. The scenario deliberately makes Ms. Iyer both WTD AND CFO to test whether students know the membership restriction.

questions.question: Dr. Rajan Pillai was appointed as an Independent Director in March 2016, completed his first 5-year term in March 2021, was reappointed for a second term ending March 2026, and is now retiring. He is currently Chairman of the Audit Committee. Regarding Dr. Pillai's tenure and any post-retirement restrictions, which of the following is INCORRECT?

options.A: Dr. Pillai has served the maximum permissible tenure of two consecutive terms of 5 years each (10 years total) as an ID, and cannot be reappointed as an independent director of NTL without a cooling-off period of 3 years
options.B: After the expiry of his second term, Dr. Pillai can be immediately reappointed as a Non-Executive Non-Independent Director of NTL without any cooling-off period, since the cooling-off restriction applies only to reappointment as an independent director
options.C: Dr. Pillai can be reappointed for a third consecutive 5-year term as an Independent Director if the company passes a special resolution and SEBI grants specific approval, since SEBI has the power to relax the two-term limit in exceptional cases
options.D: During the 3-year cooling-off period after completing two consecutive terms, Dr. Pillai cannot serve in ANY capacity (including as a consultant, advisor, or non-independent director) in NTL or any of its subsidiaries, associates, or group companies

questions.explanation: Option C is INCORRECT. There is NO provision under SEBI LODR or the Companies Act, 2013 for SEBI to grant 'specific approval' for a third consecutive term of an independent director. The two-term (5+5 = 10 years) limit is absolute, and there is no mechanism to relax it regardless of special resolution or SEBI approval. This is a fabricated exception designed to trap students who think regulatory bodies can always grant waivers. Option A is correct — Section 149(10)-(11) of the Companies Act read with SEBI LODR limits IDs to two consecutive 5-year terms with a mandatory 3-year cooling-off. Option B is correct — the cooling-off restriction specifically applies to reappointment as an INDEPENDENT director; there is no bar on appointing the person as a non-executive non-independent director immediately. Option D is the 'close but too strict' trap — during the cooling-off period, the person cannot serve as an ID, but the restriction on serving in 'ANY capacity' including as consultant or non-independent director is debatable and overly broad. However, Option C is clearly more incorrect than Option D since it fabricates a non-existent SEBI waiver power. The scenario's detail about Dr. Pillai's exact appointment dates (March 2016, reappointed March 2021) establishes the precise 10-year tenure calculation.

scenarios.scenarioText: Bharat Infrastructure Corp. Ltd. (BICL) is a listed company ranked 650th by market capitalisation (approximately Rs. 4,800 crore) on the NSE. Its consolidated turnover for FY 2025-26 was Rs. 12,500 crore. BICL's promoter group holds 52.3% equity. The company entered into the following transactions during FY 2025-26: (i) A contract worth Rs. 850 crore with Kapoor Construction Pvt. Ltd. (KCPL), a company in which BICL's Managing Director, Mr. Rajendra Kapoor's brother, Mr. Manoj Kapoor, holds 74% equity. The contract was for the construction of a highway stretch in Madhya Pradesh. (ii) A brand licensing agreement with 'Bharat Infra Solutions' (a partnership firm in which Mr. Rajendra Kapoor is a sleeping partner holding 25% share) for use of the 'Bharat' brand name at a royalty of Rs. 680 crore per annum, representing 5.44% of BICL's consolidated turnover. (iii) A loan of Rs. 120 crore extended to Zenith Realty Pvt. Ltd. (ZRPL), a company in which BICL's Independent Director, Ms. Nandini Sharma, holds 15% equity and is also a non-executive director. (iv) Purchase of office equipment worth Rs. 8 crore from Kapoor Electronics, a sole proprietorship owned by Mr. Rajendra Kapoor's son, Mr. Siddharth Kapoor (aged 23). The Audit Committee approved all four transactions. For Transaction (i) and (ii), the Board also passed resolutions. However, no shareholders' approval was sought for any transaction. BICL's Company Secretary, Mr. Hemant Patil, is now reviewing whether any of these transactions required shareholders' approval by way of special resolution, and whether Ms. Nandini Sharma's independence as a director is affected by Transaction (iii). The previous year's Audit Committee meeting discussing RPTs had quorum issues — only 2 members were present, including 1 independent director, out of a 4-member committee.

questions.question: Transaction (i) with KCPL is worth Rs. 850 crore. BICL's consolidated turnover is Rs. 12,500 crore. Under Regulation 23 of SEBI LODR, the threshold for a 'material related party transaction' is the LOWER of Rs. 1,000 crore or 10% of consolidated turnover. Which of the following CORRECTLY determines whether Transaction (i) is a 'material RPT' requiring shareholders' approval?

options.A: 10% of Rs. 12,500 crore = Rs. 1,250 crore. Since Rs. 1,250 crore > Rs. 1,000 crore, the threshold is Rs. 1,000 crore (the lower). Transaction (i) at Rs. 850 crore is below Rs. 1,000 crore, so it is NOT a material RPT and does not require shareholders' approval
options.B: 10% of Rs. 12,500 crore = Rs. 1,250 crore. The threshold is Rs. 1,250 crore (the higher). Transaction (i) at Rs. 850 crore is below Rs. 1,250 crore, so it is NOT a material RPT
options.C: 10% of Rs. 12,500 crore = Rs. 1,250 crore. Since the threshold is the LOWER of Rs. 1,000 crore or Rs. 1,250 crore = Rs. 1,000 crore, and Transaction (i) at Rs. 850 crore is below Rs. 1,000 crore, it is NOT material. However, shareholders' approval may still be required under the Companies Act, 2013 based on separate thresholds under Section 188
options.D: The materiality threshold under LODR does not apply to construction contracts — such contracts are assessed under a separate 'project value' threshold of Rs. 500 crore, and Transaction (i) at Rs. 850 crore exceeds this, making it a material RPT

questions.explanation: Option C is the BEST and most complete answer. Under Regulation 23(1) of SEBI LODR, a material RPT is one where the transaction/transactions to be entered into individually or taken together with previous transactions during a financial year exceeds the LOWER of Rs. 1,000 crore or 10% of the annual consolidated turnover. Here: 10% of Rs. 12,500 crore = Rs. 1,250 crore. The threshold is the LOWER = Rs. 1,000 crore. Transaction (i) at Rs. 850 crore is below Rs. 1,000 crore, so it is NOT a material RPT under LODR. However, Option C correctly notes that the Companies Act, 2013 (Section 188) has its own separate thresholds for RPT approval, which may still apply independently. Option A reaches the same numerical conclusion but is incomplete — it doesn't address the Companies Act dimension. Option B applies the HIGHER of the two figures, which is the classic 'higher vs lower' reversal trap. Students frequently confuse 'lower of' with 'higher of' in this regulation. Option D fabricates a 'project value threshold' for construction contracts that does not exist. The key trap is the 'LOWER of' formulation — CLAUDE.md specifically identifies this as a top trap for LODR.

questions.question: Transaction (ii) is a brand licensing/royalty agreement at Rs. 680 crore per annum, representing 5.44% of BICL's consolidated turnover. Under SEBI LODR, royalty/brand payments have a separate materiality threshold. Which of the following CORRECTLY evaluates whether Transaction (ii) requires shareholders' approval?

options.A: Royalty/brand payments to related parties are material if they exceed 5% of consolidated turnover. Here, Rs. 680 crore = 5.44% of Rs. 12,500 crore, which exceeds 5%. Therefore, Transaction (ii) IS a material RPT requiring shareholders' approval by ordinary resolution
options.B: Royalty/brand payments to related parties are material if they exceed 2% of consolidated turnover. Here, Rs. 680 crore = 5.44% which exceeds 2%. Therefore, Transaction (ii) IS a material RPT requiring shareholders' approval by special resolution
options.C: The general materiality threshold (lower of Rs. 1,000 crore or 10% turnover) applies. Rs. 680 crore is below Rs. 1,000 crore, so it is NOT a material RPT, and the 5% royalty threshold is merely a disclosure requirement, not an approval trigger
options.D: Royalty/brand payments to related parties exceeding 5% of consolidated turnover require shareholders' approval by ordinary resolution under Regulation 23, and the related party (Bharat Infra Solutions) cannot vote on this resolution

questions.explanation: Option D is the most complete and correct answer. Under Regulation 23(1A) of SEBI LODR, a transaction involving payments made to a related party with respect to brand usage or royalty shall be considered material if the transaction(s) exceeds 5% of the annual consolidated turnover as per the last audited financial statements. Here, Rs. 680 crore / Rs. 12,500 crore = 5.44%, which exceeds 5%. Therefore, it IS a material RPT requiring shareholders' approval. Additionally, under Regulation 23(4), no related party shall vote to approve such resolution. Option A correctly identifies the 5% threshold and the material status but incorrectly states 'ordinary resolution' without the related party voting restriction — it's the voting restriction that makes this provision unique. Option B fabricates a 2% threshold and incorrectly prescribes 'special resolution' — LODR requires ordinary resolution for RPT approval (not special). Option C incorrectly applies only the general threshold and dismisses the 5% royalty rule as merely a disclosure requirement. The key scenario fact is the 5.44% figure — it's deliberately set just above 5% to create a borderline scenario where students must precisely apply the threshold.

questions.question: Transaction (iii) involves a Rs. 120 crore loan to Zenith Realty Pvt. Ltd. (ZRPL), in which Independent Director Ms. Nandini Sharma holds 15% equity and is a non-executive director. Regarding the impact of this transaction on Ms. Sharma's status as an Independent Director, which of the following is CORRECT?

options.A: Ms. Sharma's independence is NOT affected because the loan is made by BICL to ZRPL (not by ZRPL to BICL), and the independent director restriction relates only to receiving pecuniary benefits FROM the company, not to the company extending benefits to entities in which the ID has an interest
options.B: Ms. Sharma's independence IS affected because she holds a 'material pecuniary relationship' with a company (ZRPL) that has a transaction with BICL exceeding 10% of ZRPL's gross turnover, and this constitutes a disqualification under the independence criteria
options.C: Ms. Sharma's independence IS potentially compromised because holding 15% equity in a company that receives a Rs. 120 crore loan from the listed company creates a material interest, and under Regulation 16(1)(b) read with Section 149(6), an ID should not have a material pecuniary relationship with the listed company or its subsidiaries, directly or INDIRECTLY
options.D: Ms. Sharma's independence is NOT affected because the 2% shareholding cap under Section 149(6) applies to shareholding in the LISTED company (BICL), not to shareholding in third-party companies; her 15% in ZRPL is irrelevant to her independence in BICL

questions.explanation: Option C is correct. Under Regulation 16(1)(b) of SEBI LODR read with Section 149(6) of the Companies Act, 2013, an independent director must not have a material pecuniary relationship with the listed company, its holding, subsidiary, or associate company, or their promoters/directors, directly or INDIRECTLY. Ms. Sharma holds 15% equity in ZRPL AND is its non-executive director. ZRPL received a Rs. 120 crore loan from BICL. This creates an INDIRECT material pecuniary relationship — Ms. Sharma benefits (as a 15% shareholder and director of ZRPL) from a financial transaction with BICL. Option A is wrong because the independence test covers both direct and indirect pecuniary relationships — it's not limited to receiving money FROM the listed company. Option B correctly identifies the concern but applies a specific '10% of ZRPL's gross turnover' test that is not the exact statutory language — the test is 'material pecuniary relationship' which is broader. Option D narrowly reads the 2% cap (which relates to voting power in the listed company) and ignores the broader 'material pecuniary relationship' test. The scenario deliberately makes Ms. Sharma BOTH a shareholder (15%) AND director of ZRPL to strengthen the indirect relationship argument.

questions.question: The Audit Committee meeting that discussed RPTs had only 2 members present out of 4, including just 1 independent director. Under Regulation 18(2) of SEBI LODR, which of the following CORRECTLY evaluates the quorum for the Audit Committee?

options.A: The quorum was met because Regulation 18 requires a minimum of 2 members for quorum, and 2 members were present
options.B: The quorum was NOT met because Regulation 18(2) requires a quorum of 2 members OR one-third of the members, WHICHEVER IS GREATER, with a minimum of 2 independent directors; here, one-third of 4 = 1.33, rounded up to 2, so quorum is 2 members — but only 1 ID was present, violating the minimum 2 IDs requirement
options.C: The quorum was met because the quorum requirement is simply a majority of members (3 out of 4), and since only 2 were present, the meeting was inquorate — but this is under the Companies Act, not LODR
options.D: The quorum was NOT met because Regulation 18 requires ALL members of the Audit Committee to be present when discussing related party transactions, as RPTs require unanimous approval by the Audit Committee

questions.explanation: Under Regulation 18(2) of SEBI LODR, the quorum for an Audit Committee meeting shall be either 2 members or one-third of the members of the Audit Committee, WHICHEVER IS GREATER, with a minimum of 2 independent directors present. For a 4-member Audit Committee: one-third of 4 = 1.33, rounded up to 2. So the quorum requirement is 2 members (which is equal to one-third rounded up). However, the additional requirement is that at least 2 independent directors must be present at the meeting. In this case, only 1 independent director was present. Therefore, the quorum was NOT met despite having 2 members present, because the minimum 2 IDs requirement was violated. Option A correctly calculates the numerical quorum (2 members) but ignores the critical '2 IDs minimum' requirement. Option C introduces a majority quorum concept from the Companies Act which is not the LODR standard. Option D fabricates a unanimity requirement for RPT discussions. The scenario deliberately presents a situation where the number of members meets the threshold but the ID-specific quorum does not — testing whether students know BOTH components of the quorum rule.

questions.question: BICL is ranked 650th by market capitalisation on NSE. Under SEBI LODR, certain governance requirements apply only to the top 1,000 or top 2,000 listed entities by market capitalisation. Which of the following committees or requirements is BICL mandatorily required to constitute/comply with, given its ranking?

options.A: BICL must constitute a Risk Management Committee because it is within the top 1,000 listed entities; it must also separate the roles of Chairman and MD, with the Chairperson being a non-executive director
options.B: BICL is NOT required to constitute a Risk Management Committee because this requirement applies only to the top 500 listed entities by market capitalisation, and BICL is ranked 650th
options.C: BICL must constitute a Risk Management Committee (top 1,000), but it is NOT required to have an independent woman director on the board since that requirement applies only to the top 500 listed entities
options.D: BICL must constitute a Risk Management Committee (top 1,000 requirement under Regulation 21), but requirements like mandatory separation of Chairman/MD roles and additional independent director criteria apply only to the top 500 or top 250 entities, not to entities ranked 650th

questions.explanation: Option D is correct. Under Regulation 21 of SEBI LODR, the top 1,000 listed entities by market capitalisation are mandatorily required to constitute a Risk Management Committee. Since BICL is ranked 650th, it falls within this requirement. However, stricter governance norms like mandatory separation of Chairman and MD roles (Regulation 17(1B)) and additional ID requirements apply to the top 500 or top 250 entities — not to BICL at rank 650. Option A correctly identifies the Risk Management Committee requirement but incorrectly states that separation of Chairman/MD roles is mandatory for all top 1,000 entities — this applies to a more restricted subset. Option B is wrong — the Risk Management Committee requirement is for the top 1,000, not top 500. Option C incorrectly states that an independent woman director requirement applies only to the top 500 — actually, every listed entity must have at least one woman director (Regulation 17), and the top 500/1000 may have additional requirements. The scenario deliberately places BICL at rank 650 — within top 1,000 (so Risk Management Committee applies) but outside top 500 (so stricter requirements don't apply).

scenarios.scenarioText: Orion Pharmaceuticals Ltd. (OPL) is a listed company with a market capitalisation of Rs. 22,000 crore, consolidated turnover of Rs. 9,800 crore, and promoter holding of 41.6%. OPL's financial year ends on March 31. For FY 2025-26, the following timeline of events occurred: (a) The Board met on May 12, 2026, to approve the standalone quarterly financial results for Q4 (January–March 2026) and the annual audited standalone financial results for FY 2025-26. The statutory auditor, M/s. Krishnan & Associates, issued an audit report with a 'qualified opinion' due to a dispute over revenue recognition of Rs. 340 crore from a government contract. (b) The Board approved the consolidated annual results on May 18, 2026 — 6 days after the standalone results. (c) The Annual General Meeting (AGM) was held on September 25, 2026. The annual report was sent to shareholders on October 2, 2026. (d) The corporate governance report for Q4 FY 2025-26 was filed with the stock exchanges on May 8, 2026. (e) During Q3 (October–December 2025), OPL had disclosed to the stock exchanges under Regulation 30 that it received a show-cause notice from the Drug Controller General of India (DCGI) regarding alleged clinical trial irregularities for its flagship drug 'CardioShield.' The disclosure was made within 24 hours of receipt. However, in February 2026, the DCGI dropped all charges, and OPL disclosed the outcome on March 5, 2026 — 18 days after the DCGI order dated February 15, 2026. (f) OPL's Compliance Officer, Mr. Vikram Shetty, is also serving as the Company Secretary. He was on medical leave from April 15 to May 20, 2026, during which period no compliance officer was designated. The stock exchanges issued a warning letter regarding the delayed disclosure of the DCGI outcome.

questions.question: OPL's Board approved the Q4/annual standalone financial results on May 12, 2026 — 42 days after the end of the financial year (March 31, 2026). Under Regulation 33 of SEBI LODR, which of the following CORRECTLY evaluates the timeliness of this approval?

options.A: Compliant for quarterly results (45-day deadline) but non-compliant for annual results (30-day deadline for annual audited results from the end of the financial year)
options.B: Non-compliant for both — quarterly results must be approved within 30 days and annual results within 45 days of the end of the financial year
options.C: Compliant for quarterly results (45-day deadline) but non-compliant for annual results (60-day deadline for annual audited results from the end of the financial year) — wait, 42 days is within 60 days, so it IS compliant for annual results as well
options.D: The quarterly results deadline of 45 days does not apply to Q4 because Q4 results are subsumed within the annual results; only the 60-day deadline for annual results applies, and at 42 days, OPL is compliant

questions.explanation: Under Regulation 33 of SEBI LODR: quarterly financial results must be submitted within 45 days from the end of the quarter, and annual AUDITED financial results must be submitted within 60 days from the end of the financial year. For Q4 (ending March 31): standalone quarterly results approved on May 12 = 42 days — within the 45-day deadline (COMPLIANT). For annual results: approved on May 12 = 42 days — within the 60-day deadline (COMPLIANT). Option C correctly walks through the analysis, initially second-guessing but arriving at the right conclusion that both are compliant. Option A is the most tempting trap — it fabricates a '30-day' deadline for annual results. Students commonly confuse 45 days (quarterly) with 60 days (annual). Option B reverses the two deadlines entirely — 30 for quarterly and 45 for annual — both wrong. Option D raises an interesting point about Q4 being subsumed in annual results, and while there is some truth to Q4/annual overlap, the question tests whether students know both the 45-day and 60-day deadlines. The scenario's 42-day figure is deliberately set to be within both deadlines, making the question about knowledge of the deadlines rather than computation.

questions.question: OPL's annual report was sent to shareholders on October 2, 2026 — 7 days after the AGM held on September 25, 2026. Under Regulation 34 of SEBI LODR, which of the following CORRECTLY evaluates the compliance of annual report submission?

options.A: Non-compliant because the annual report must be sent to shareholders at least 21 days BEFORE the AGM (as notice period), not after; sending it 7 days after the AGM defeats its purpose
options.B: Compliant because Regulation 34 requires the annual report to be submitted to the stock exchanges within 21 working days of the AGM, and 7 calendar days is well within 21 working days
options.C: Non-compliant because Regulation 34 requires the annual report to be submitted within 21 CALENDAR days (not working days) of it being approved by the Board, and the report was sent 7 days after the AGM — but the question is when the Board approved it, not when the AGM was held
options.D: Non-compliant because the annual report must be filed with the stock exchanges on the same day as the AGM, along with the AGM proceedings and voting results

questions.explanation: Under Regulation 34(1) of SEBI LODR, the annual report shall be submitted to the stock exchange within 21 working days of it being approved and adopted at the AGM. The annual report was adopted at the AGM on September 25, 2026, and submitted on October 2, 2026 — 7 calendar days later, which is well within 21 WORKING days. Option B is correct. Option A confuses the AGM notice period (which requires sending the notice and annual report to shareholders BEFORE the AGM) with the post-AGM filing requirement under Regulation 34. While the annual report is indeed sent to shareholders before the AGM as part of the notice, Regulation 34 specifically deals with the stock exchange submission timeline AFTER the AGM. Option C incorrectly refers to 'calendar days' and Board approval — Regulation 34 uses 'working days' and the trigger is AGM adoption, not Board approval. Option D fabricates a same-day filing requirement. The scenario's mention of 'sent to shareholders on October 2' after the AGM tests whether students differentiate between the pre-AGM circulation (notice period) and post-AGM filing (Regulation 34).

questions.question: OPL filed the Q4 FY 2025-26 corporate governance report with the stock exchanges on May 8, 2026. Under Regulation 27 of SEBI LODR, what is the deadline for filing the corporate governance report, and is OPL's filing compliant?

options.A: The corporate governance report must be filed within 15 days from the end of each quarter. Q4 ends March 31, so the deadline is April 15. Filing on May 8 (38 days later) is NON-COMPLIANT
options.B: The corporate governance report must be filed within 21 days from the end of each quarter. Q4 ends March 31, so the deadline is April 21. Filing on May 8 (38 days later) is NON-COMPLIANT
options.C: The corporate governance report must be filed within 30 days from the end of each quarter. Q4 ends March 31, so the deadline is April 30. Filing on May 8 (38 days later) is NON-COMPLIANT
options.D: The corporate governance report must be filed along with the quarterly financial results, and since OPL's Q4 financial results were approved on May 12, filing the governance report on May 8 (before the results) is non-compliant because it should have been filed simultaneously

questions.explanation: Under Regulation 27(2) of SEBI LODR, the listed entity shall submit a quarterly compliance report on corporate governance within 21 days from the close of the quarter. Q4 FY 2025-26 ends on March 31, 2026. The deadline is March 31 + 21 days = April 21, 2026. OPL filed on May 8, 2026 — 38 days after quarter-end, which is 17 days beyond the deadline. This is NON-COMPLIANT. Option A uses 15 days (too short). Option C uses 30 days (too long — students often confuse this with other filing deadlines). Option D incorrectly links the governance report filing to the financial results timeline — they are independent filings with separate deadlines. The 21-day deadline for corporate governance reports is a frequently tested number that students confuse with: 45 days (quarterly financials), 60 days (annual financials), or 30 days (other filings). The scenario deliberately places the filing on May 8 — after all three potential deadlines (15, 21, and 30 days) — so only students who know the exact 21-day deadline will correctly identify it as non-compliant and by how much.

questions.question: The DCGI dropped all charges against OPL on February 15, 2026, but OPL disclosed this outcome to the stock exchanges on March 5, 2026 — 18 days later. Under Regulation 30 of SEBI LODR regarding disclosure of material events, which of the following is CORRECT?

options.A: The disclosure is compliant because Regulation 30 requires disclosure within 30 days of a material event, and 18 days is within this period
options.B: The disclosure is non-compliant because Regulation 30 requires disclosure of material events or information as soon as reasonably possible and not later than 24 hours from the occurrence of the event; the 18-day delay is a clear violation
options.C: The disclosure is compliant because the DCGI dropping charges is a POSITIVE development, and Regulation 30 mandates prompt disclosure only for adverse events that may impact share price negatively
options.D: The disclosure is not required at all because the DCGI dropping charges merely reverts the company to its pre-notice status, and Regulation 30 only requires disclosure of 'new' material events, not the resolution of previously disclosed events

questions.explanation: Under Regulation 30 of SEBI LODR, a listed entity shall disclose material events or information as soon as reasonably possible and not later than 24 hours from the occurrence of the event or information. The DCGI dropping all charges is a material event — it directly impacts investor perception (especially since the original show-cause notice was disclosed). OPL took 18 days to disclose this, which far exceeds the 24-hour deadline. This is clearly NON-COMPLIANT. Option A fabricates a 30-day window — no such extended period exists for material event disclosure under Regulation 30. Option C wrongly suggests that only adverse events require prompt disclosure — Regulation 30 applies to ALL material events, whether positive or negative, that could impact the share price or investor decisions. A positive development like charges being dropped is price-sensitive information that investors need promptly. Option D is legally incorrect — the outcome of a previously disclosed event is itself a material event requiring disclosure. The scenario deliberately mentions that OPL had previously disclosed the show-cause notice within 24 hours (compliant), creating a contrast with the 18-day delay in disclosing the favorable outcome. The stock exchange's warning letter confirms the non-compliance.

questions.question: OPL's statutory auditor issued a qualified opinion on the annual financial results due to a Rs. 340 crore revenue recognition dispute. Under SEBI LODR, which of the following CORRECTLY describes the listed entity's obligations when the auditor's report contains a qualification?

options.A: The Board must provide a detailed explanation for each audit qualification in the annual report, quantifying the financial impact of each qualification on the profit/loss and net worth, and the audit committee must also comment on the qualification
options.B: The company must appoint a different statutory auditor for the next financial year because a qualified opinion indicates a breakdown of the auditor-company relationship, and SEBI LODR mandates auditor rotation after any qualification
options.C: The company must disclose the qualified opinion to the stock exchanges within 48 hours as a material event under Regulation 30, but no further action is required until the next AGM where the auditor's report is presented to shareholders
options.D: The company must submit a revised financial result excluding the disputed Rs. 340 crore revenue within 30 days, as the qualified opinion renders the original submission incomplete under Regulation 33

questions.explanation: Under SEBI LODR (Regulation 33(3)(d) and related provisions), when the auditor's report contains a qualification, the Board of Directors must provide a detailed explanation for each audit qualification in the annual report. The company must quantify the financial impact of each qualification on the profit/loss and net worth. The audit committee is also required to comment on each qualification. This 'statement on impact of audit qualifications' is a standard disclosure requirement for listed entities. Option B is completely wrong — a qualified opinion does NOT mandate auditor change; auditor rotation is governed by separate provisions under the Companies Act, and a qualification alone does not trigger rotation. Option C understates the obligation — while disclosure under Regulation 30 may apply, the primary obligation is the detailed explanation and quantification of impact in the annual report, not just a stock exchange disclosure. Option D fabricates a requirement for 'revised financial results' — a qualified opinion does not require restatement; rather, the Board must explain the qualification and its impact. The scenario's specific mention of 'Rs. 340 crore revenue recognition dispute' is relevant because the company must quantify how excluding this Rs. 340 crore would impact profit/loss and net worth.

scenarios.scenarioText: Meridian Financial Services Ltd. (MFSL) is a listed NBFC with a market capitalisation of Rs. 15,600 crore, consolidated turnover of Rs. 6,200 crore, and is ranked within the top 250 listed entities on NSE. MFSL's promoter group (the Chandra family) holds 58.4% equity. The Board comprises 10 directors: 4 executive (including the Executive Chairman Mr. Vikram Chandra), 2 non-executive non-independent, and 4 independent directors. MFSL entered into a contract with Chandra Finance Pvt. Ltd. (CFPL) — a 100% promoter-family-owned company — for outsourcing its entire loan recovery operations at a fee of Rs. 1,100 crore per annum. This amounts to 17.7% of MFSL's consolidated turnover. The Audit Committee approved the transaction with a 3:1 vote (3 IDs voting in favour, 1 non-executive non-independent director voting against). The Board then approved it unanimously. The Company Secretary placed the transaction for shareholders' approval at an Extraordinary General Meeting (EGM). At the EGM, the following votes were cast: (a) Promoter group (58.4%): voted FOR; (b) LIC (holding 7.2%): voted FOR; (c) Mutual funds (holding 12.8%): voted AGAINST; (d) Retail shareholders present (representing 5.6% of total equity): voted FOR (3.8%) and AGAINST (1.8%). The Company Secretary declared the resolution as passed with 66.4% votes in favour. However, Mr. Anand Rao, a minority shareholder holding 0.3%, filed a complaint with SEBI alleging that the promoter group was not entitled to vote on this resolution and the resolution should be treated as failed. MFSL also failed to disclose the RPT transaction to the stock exchanges within the prescribed timeline, disclosing it only 5 days after the Audit Committee approval. Additionally, during the same quarter, MFSL's wholly-owned subsidiary, Meridian Housing Finance Ltd. (MHFL), entered into a Rs. 450 crore loan arrangement with CFPL — another related party transaction at the subsidiary level.

questions.question: The outsourcing contract with CFPL is worth Rs. 1,100 crore against MFSL's consolidated turnover of Rs. 6,200 crore. Under Regulation 23 of SEBI LODR, is this transaction a 'material RPT,' and if so, what threshold was breached?

options.A: Material RPT: the transaction (Rs. 1,100 crore) exceeds the threshold of Rs. 1,000 crore (being the LOWER of Rs. 1,000 crore or 10% of Rs. 6,200 crore = Rs. 620 crore); however, since 10% = Rs. 620 crore is LOWER than Rs. 1,000 crore, the actual threshold is Rs. 620 crore, and the transaction exceeds both
options.B: Material RPT: the threshold is the HIGHER of Rs. 1,000 crore or 10% of turnover (Rs. 620 crore) = Rs. 1,000 crore; the transaction at Rs. 1,100 crore exceeds Rs. 1,000 crore
options.C: NOT a material RPT: 10% of turnover = Rs. 620 crore, and Rs. 1,000 crore is the cap; since Rs. 1,100 crore exceeds the cap, the transaction is treated as an ordinary business transaction not requiring special approval
options.D: Material RPT: the threshold is the LOWER of Rs. 1,000 crore or 10% of Rs. 6,200 crore = Rs. 620 crore; since Rs. 1,100 crore far exceeds Rs. 620 crore (the applicable threshold), shareholders' approval is required

questions.explanation: Under Regulation 23(1), a material RPT is one exceeding the LOWER of Rs. 1,000 crore or 10% of annual consolidated turnover. Here: 10% of Rs. 6,200 crore = Rs. 620 crore. The LOWER of Rs. 1,000 crore and Rs. 620 crore = Rs. 620 crore. The transaction at Rs. 1,100 crore far exceeds Rs. 620 crore — it is clearly a material RPT requiring shareholders' approval. Option D correctly applies the 'LOWER of' formula. Option A correctly identifies Rs. 620 crore as the threshold but the reasoning is muddled — it says 'exceeds the threshold of Rs. 1,000 crore' first, then corrects to Rs. 620 crore, showing confused analysis. Option B applies 'HIGHER of' instead of 'LOWER of' — the classic reversal trap. The correct threshold is Rs. 620 crore (the lower), not Rs. 1,000 crore. Option C fabricates a 'cap' concept that converts large transactions into ordinary business — this is nonsensical. This question reinforces the 'LOWER of' concept from Scenario 2 but with a different turnover figure, ensuring students can apply the formula regardless of the specific numbers.

questions.question: At the EGM, the Company Secretary declared the RPT resolution passed with 66.4% votes in favour (including the promoter group's 58.4%). Mr. Anand Rao alleges the promoter group should not have voted. Under Regulation 23(4) of SEBI LODR, which of the following CORRECTLY evaluates whether the resolution was validly passed?

options.A: The resolution is validly passed because Regulation 23(4) bars only the RELATED PARTY from voting, not the entire promoter group; CFPL (the counterparty) did not vote, so the promoter group's votes are valid
options.B: The resolution is NOT validly passed because under Regulation 23(4), no RELATED PARTY shall vote to approve a material RPT, and since the Chandra family controls both MFSL (as promoters) and CFPL (100% ownership), they are the 'related party' and their 58.4% votes must be excluded — leaving only 8% FOR (LIC 7.2% + retail 0.8% of the 3.8%), which is less than the 17.6% AGAINST (MF 12.8% + retail 1.8% + promoter's excluded portion adjusting denominator)
options.C: The resolution is validly passed because Regulation 23(4) only applies to transactions exceeding Rs. 1,000 crore, and since the effective threshold here is Rs. 620 crore, the voting restriction does not apply
options.D: The resolution is NOT validly passed, but only because a material RPT requires approval by SPECIAL resolution (75% majority), and 66.4% does not meet the 75% threshold — the promoter voting issue is irrelevant since all shareholders can vote on RPTs

questions.explanation: Option B is correct. Under Regulation 23(4) of SEBI LODR, no related party shall vote to approve the resolution, whether the entity is a related party to the particular transaction or not. The Chandra family (promoter group) controls BOTH MFSL (58.4% equity) and CFPL (100% ownership). As the related party, the promoter group's votes (58.4%) must be EXCLUDED from the voting. Excluding the promoter group's 58.4% from the denominator, the effective votes are: FOR = LIC 7.2% + retail FOR 3.8% = 11%; AGAINST = MFs 12.8% + retail AGAINST 1.8% = 14.6%. With more votes AGAINST than FOR (among eligible voters), the resolution FAILS. Option A incorrectly narrows the voting restriction to only the 'counterparty entity' (CFPL) — Regulation 23(4) uses the broader term 'related party' which includes the promoter group that controls the counterparty. Option C fabricates a Rs. 1,000 crore threshold for the voting restriction — the voting restriction applies to ALL material RPTs regardless of the absolute value. Option D incorrectly requires a 'special resolution' — LODR requires an ordinary resolution for RPT approval, not a special resolution. The key scenario fact is the 100% ownership of CFPL by the Chandra family — this makes the promoter group unambiguously a 'related party' to the transaction.

questions.question: MFSL is ranked within the top 250 listed entities by market capitalisation. Its board has 10 directors: 4 executive (including the Executive Chairman), 2 non-executive non-independent, and 4 independent directors. Under Regulation 17 as applicable to top 250 entities, which of the following identifies ALL the governance non-compliances?

options.A: Only one non-compliance: with an executive chairman, at least 5 IDs are needed (half of 10) but only 4 are present
options.B: Two non-compliances: (i) at least 5 IDs are needed (half of 10 for executive chairman) but only 4 are present, and (ii) the chairperson of a top 250 entity should ideally be a non-executive director, but Mr. Vikram Chandra is executive
options.C: No non-compliance: 4 IDs constitute exactly one-third of 12 directors if 2 are co-opted, and the one-third threshold applies since Mr. Chandra is a promoter-executive which is treated as a non-executive for LODR purposes
options.D: Only one non-compliance: the board should have at least 6 non-executive directors (50% of board), and currently only 6 are non-executive (2 non-executive non-independent + 4 IDs = 6), so the 50% non-executive requirement is met, but the ID-specific count of 4 out of 10 (40%) falls short of the 50% requirement

questions.explanation: Under Regulation 17(1)(b), where the chairperson is an executive director, at least HALF the board must be independent directors. With 10 directors, the minimum is 5 IDs. MFSL has only 4 IDs — this is a clear non-compliance (shortfall of 1 ID). Option A correctly identifies this as the key non-compliance. Option B adds a second non-compliance about the chairperson needing to be non-executive for top 250 entities. While Regulation 17(1B) does state that for top 500 entities (which includes top 250), the chairperson shall not be related to the MD or CEO, and the roles should be separated — the regulation doesn't absolutely prohibit an executive chairman. The provision relating to non-executive chairperson applies specifically to entities where the MD/CEO is a separate person, requiring role separation. Since Mr. Chandra is himself the Executive Chairman (combined role), the analysis is more nuanced. Option A captures the clearest, most definitive non-compliance. Option C fabricates a co-option concept and misapplies the threshold. Option D correctly computes the non-executive count (6 out of 10 = 60%) but then arrives at the right conclusion through the ID-specific test — however, it states the requirement is '50% non-executive' which confuses the NE requirement with the ID requirement. The ID shortfall (4 vs 5 required) is the definitive non-compliance.

questions.question: MFSL's wholly-owned subsidiary MHFL entered into a Rs. 450 crore loan arrangement with CFPL. Under Regulation 23 of SEBI LODR regarding RPTs at the subsidiary level, which of the following is CORRECT?

options.A: The subsidiary's RPT does not require approval from MFSL's Board or shareholders because MHFL is a separate legal entity with its own board, and the RPT provisions under LODR apply only to the listed entity, not its subsidiaries
options.B: The subsidiary's RPT requires prior approval of MFSL's Audit Committee, and if it qualifies as a material RPT (applying the same threshold as MFSL), it also requires MFSL shareholders' approval — because Regulation 23 extends to RPTs of unlisted subsidiaries of listed entities
options.C: The subsidiary's RPT requires only MHFL's own Audit Committee approval and does not need to go to MFSL's Audit Committee or shareholders, since MHFL is a wholly-owned subsidiary and the parent company is insulated from subsidiary-level transactions
options.D: The subsidiary's RPT must be approved by the RBI (since MFSL is an NBFC) before any corporate governance approval under LODR, and SEBI LODR provisions are subordinate to RBI regulations for NBFCs

questions.explanation: Under Regulation 23(2)/(2A) of SEBI LODR, all related party transactions of UNLISTED SUBSIDIARIES of listed entities also require prior approval of the Audit Committee of the LISTED entity. If the subsidiary's RPT qualifies as a material RPT (applying the thresholds), it requires shareholders' approval of the listed entity as well. This is because SEBI extended the RPT governance framework to subsidiaries to prevent listed entities from routing transactions through subsidiaries to avoid oversight. Option B correctly captures this. Option A is the most common trap — students assume that because a subsidiary is a separate legal entity, the parent's governance norms don't apply. Regulation 23 specifically extends to unlisted subsidiaries. Option C makes the same error as Option A but adds a 'wholly-owned subsidiary insulation' concept that does not exist — in fact, being wholly-owned makes the governance concern GREATER since the listed entity fully controls the subsidiary. Option D incorrectly subordinates SEBI LODR to RBI regulations — while RBI regulations do apply to NBFCs, SEBI LODR governance requirements apply independently and concurrently. The scenario's mention of MHFL being a wholly-owned subsidiary is relevant because it establishes MFSL's control, reinforcing why MFSL's Audit Committee oversight is necessary.

questions.question: MFSL disclosed the RPT transaction to the stock exchanges 5 days after the Audit Committee approval. Under Regulation 30 of SEBI LODR regarding disclosure of material events, and considering that the transaction qualifies as a material RPT, which of the following is CORRECT?

options.A: The disclosure is compliant because RPTs are required to be disclosed in the quarterly corporate governance report under Regulation 27, not as individual event-based disclosures under Regulation 30
options.B: The disclosure is non-compliant because Regulation 30 read with Schedule III requires disclosure of material RPTs as soon as reasonably possible and not later than 24 hours from approval by the Board or Audit Committee; a 5-day delay violates this timeline
options.C: The disclosure is compliant because RPT-related disclosures have a 7-day window under Regulation 23(9) which is a specific provision that overrides the general 24-hour rule under Regulation 30
options.D: The disclosure is non-compliant, but the 5-day delay is condonable without penalty because the transaction was subsequently placed before shareholders for approval, and the eventual shareholder approval cures any interim disclosure deficiency

questions.explanation: Under Regulation 30 read with Part A of Schedule III of SEBI LODR, agreements with related parties (material RPTs) are classified as material events/information that must be disclosed to the stock exchanges as soon as reasonably possible and not later than 24 hours from the occurrence (which includes Board/Audit Committee approval). MFSL's 5-day delay clearly violates this 24-hour requirement. Option A incorrectly suggests that RPTs are only disclosed through quarterly governance reports — while quarterly reporting exists under Regulation 27, event-based disclosure under Regulation 30 is a separate, immediate obligation. Option C fabricates a '7-day window' under Regulation 23(9) — no such specific extended timeline exists for RPT disclosures. Option D incorrectly suggests that subsequent shareholder approval 'cures' the disclosure delay — timely disclosure is an independent obligation, and subsequent approval does not retroactively make the delayed disclosure compliant. The scenario deliberately mentions the 5-day delay to test whether students know the 24-hour standard under Regulation 30 applies to RPT approvals.

scenarios.scenarioText: DataVault Technologies Ltd. (DVTL) is a listed IT services company ranked 180th by market capitalisation (approximately Rs. 28,500 crore) with a consolidated turnover of Rs. 11,200 crore and promoter holding of 32.8%. The company has an Audit Committee comprising 4 members: Ms. Rekha Srinivasan (ID, Chairperson), Mr. Arun Khanna (ID), Dr. Pankaj Bhatt (ID), and Mr. Gopal Krishnan (Non-Executive Non-Independent Director, nominee of a PE fund holding 9.5%). During Q3 FY 2025-26, the Audit Committee met on January 10, 2026 to review the following matters: (a) Approval of a related party transaction between DVTL and CyberNest Solutions Pvt. Ltd. (CSPL), a company in which DVTL's MD, Mr. Nikhil Agarwal, holds 45% equity. The transaction involved DVTL outsourcing its cybersecurity operations to CSPL at Rs. 85 crore per annum. (b) Review of the internal audit report which flagged that DVTL's subsidiary in Singapore — DataVault Asia Pte. Ltd. — had entered into a transaction worth SGD 12 million (approximately Rs. 75 crore) with a company controlled by the wife of DVTL's CFO, Mr. Rajesh Menon, without prior Audit Committee approval. (c) A whistleblower complaint received through DVTL's vigil mechanism alleging that the promoter group had been diverting company funds through a chain of shell companies to acquire personal real estate in Dubai. The whistleblower, identified as Mr. Sanjay Kumar (a senior manager in the finance department), alleged that approximately Rs. 220 crore had been siphoned over 3 years. (d) The statutory auditor's limited review report for Q3, which contained an emphasis of matter paragraph regarding a Rs. 180 crore receivable from a government entity that was overdue by 14 months. At the meeting, only 3 members were present: Ms. Srinivasan (ID), Mr. Khanna (ID), and Mr. Krishnan (Non-Executive Non-Independent). Dr. Bhatt was absent due to a family emergency. Mr. Nikhil Agarwal (MD) attended as an invitee for item (a) but left before voting. The meeting lasted 45 minutes. Following the meeting, DVTL submitted its Q3 financial results to the stock exchanges on February 18, 2026 — 49 days after the end of Q3 (December 31, 2025). The Compliance Officer filed the corporate governance report on January 25, 2026.

questions.question: At the Audit Committee meeting on January 10, 2026, only 3 out of 4 members were present: Ms. Srinivasan (ID), Mr. Khanna (ID), and Mr. Krishnan (Non-Exec Non-Independent). Under Regulation 18(2) of SEBI LODR, was the quorum met for the Audit Committee?

options.A: YES — quorum is 2 members or one-third of the total members, whichever is greater, with minimum 2 IDs; here, 2/3 of 4 = 1.33 (rounded to 2); 3 members including 2 IDs are present — all conditions met
options.B: NO — quorum requires at least 3 independent directors for a 4-member committee, and only 2 IDs were present
options.C: YES — quorum is simply a majority (3 out of 4), and since 3 members are present, the quorum is met; the ID-specific requirement is only for voting, not quorum
options.D: NO — quorum requires ALL members to be present when the Audit Committee discusses related party transactions and whistleblower complaints, as these are classified as 'sensitive matters' requiring full attendance

questions.explanation: Under Regulation 18(2) of SEBI LODR, the quorum for an Audit Committee meeting is 2 members or one-third of the members, whichever is GREATER, with a minimum of 2 independent directors. For a 4-member committee: one-third of 4 = 1.33, rounded up to 2. So the numerical quorum is 2 members. The additional requirement is minimum 2 IDs. Here: 3 members present (meets 2-member threshold), including 2 IDs (Ms. Srinivasan and Mr. Khanna — meets 2-ID minimum). ALL quorum conditions are satisfied. Option B fabricates a requirement of 3 IDs — the minimum is 2 IDs, not 3. Option C correctly concludes quorum is met but for the wrong reason — it uses a 'majority' standard which is not the LODR standard. Option D fabricates a 'full attendance for sensitive matters' requirement that doesn't exist. This question contrasts with Q9 (Scenario 2) where quorum was NOT met because only 1 ID was present despite 2 members being present — here, 2 IDs are present and quorum IS met. Testing the same rule with opposite outcomes ensures students understand both components.

questions.question: DVTL submitted its Q3 financial results on February 18, 2026 — 49 days after Q3 ended (December 31, 2025). The corporate governance report was filed on January 25, 2026 — 25 days after quarter-end. Which of the following CORRECTLY evaluates the compliance of BOTH filings?

options.A: Both are compliant: Q3 financial results within the 60-day deadline, and corporate governance report within the 30-day deadline
options.B: Financial results are NON-COMPLIANT (49 days exceeds the 45-day deadline); corporate governance report is also NON-COMPLIANT (25 days exceeds the 21-day deadline)
options.C: Financial results are NON-COMPLIANT (49 days exceeds the 45-day deadline for quarterly results); corporate governance report is COMPLIANT (25 days is within the 30-day deadline)
options.D: Financial results are COMPLIANT (49 days is within the 60-day deadline which applies to Q3 as it is the third quarter); corporate governance report is NON-COMPLIANT (25 days exceeds the 21-day deadline)

questions.explanation: Under Regulation 33, quarterly financial results must be submitted within 45 days from the end of the quarter. Q3 ends December 31; 45 days = February 14. Filing on February 18 (49 days) exceeds the deadline by 4 days — NON-COMPLIANT. Under Regulation 27(2), the corporate governance report must be submitted within 21 days from the close of the quarter. Q3 ends December 31; 21 days = January 21. Filing on January 25 (25 days) exceeds the deadline by 4 days — NON-COMPLIANT. Option A uses wrong deadlines (60 days and 30 days). The 60-day deadline applies only to ANNUAL financial results, not quarterly. Option C correctly identifies the financial results violation but uses a 30-day deadline for the governance report instead of the correct 21 days. Option D applies the 60-day annual deadline to Q3 quarterly results (wrong) and correctly identifies the governance report violation. Both deadlines — 45 days for quarterly financials and 21 days for corporate governance report — are among the most frequently confused numbers in LODR. The scenario tests both simultaneously.

questions.question: The internal audit report flagged that DVTL's Singapore subsidiary entered into a Rs. 75 crore transaction with a company controlled by the CFO's wife WITHOUT prior Audit Committee approval. Under SEBI LODR provisions regarding RPTs at the subsidiary level, which of the following CORRECTLY identifies the compliance failures?

options.A: No compliance failure at the listed entity level — the Singapore subsidiary is governed by Singapore law, and SEBI LODR has no extraterritorial application to foreign subsidiaries' related party transactions
options.B: Compliance failure: under Regulation 23, RPTs of unlisted subsidiaries (including foreign subsidiaries) require prior approval of the listed entity's Audit Committee; the Singapore subsidiary's transaction should have been approved by DVTL's Audit Committee before execution
options.C: Compliance failure, but only a disclosure violation — the transaction should have been disclosed to the stock exchanges within 24 hours; prior Audit Committee approval of the listed entity is not required for foreign subsidiary RPTs below Rs. 100 crore
options.D: No compliance failure because the CFO's wife is not a 'related party' of DVTL — she is related to the CFO personally, and the RPT framework covers only transactions with entities related to directors and promoters, not KMPs' family members

questions.explanation: Under Regulation 23(2) of SEBI LODR, ALL related party transactions of unlisted subsidiaries (including foreign subsidiaries) require prior approval of the Audit Committee of the listed entity. The Singapore subsidiary's transaction with a company controlled by the CFO's wife should have been placed before DVTL's Audit Committee for prior approval. The CFO is a Key Managerial Personnel, and his wife's company constitutes a related party under the definition. Option A wrongly claims SEBI LODR has no extraterritorial application — Regulation 23 specifically extends RPT governance to all subsidiaries regardless of jurisdiction. Option C understates the requirement — prior Audit Committee approval is mandatory, not just disclosure, and there is no Rs. 100 crore exemption threshold for foreign subsidiary RPTs. Option D incorrectly excludes KMPs' relatives from the related party definition — under the Companies Act, 2013 (Section 2(76)) read with SEBI LODR, relatives of KMPs (including spouse) are related parties. The scenario deliberately places the subsidiary in Singapore to test whether students know that LODR's RPT framework extends beyond domestic subsidiaries.

questions.question: A whistleblower complaint was received alleging Rs. 220 crore fund diversion by the promoter group. Under Regulation 22 of SEBI LODR (Vigil Mechanism), which of the following statements about the handling of this complaint is INCORRECT?

options.A: The Audit Committee must oversee the vigil mechanism, and the whistleblower Mr. Sanjay Kumar must be protected from any adverse employment action as a consequence of filing the complaint
options.B: The identity of the whistleblower (Mr. Sanjay Kumar) must be kept confidential and cannot be disclosed to the promoter group or any person against whom the complaint is made, unless required by law
options.C: The complaint must be referred to the company's internal audit team headed by the CFO Mr. Rajesh Menon for preliminary investigation before the Audit Committee reviews it, as the Audit Committee cannot directly investigate operational matters
options.D: Direct access to the chairperson of the Audit Committee must be available to employees who wish to report concerns about unethical behavior, actual or suspected fraud, or violation of the company's code of conduct

questions.explanation: Option C is INCORRECT. The vigil mechanism under Regulation 22 of SEBI LODR specifically provides for the Audit Committee to oversee the mechanism and handle complaints. The complaint should NOT be referred to the CFO's internal audit team as a prerequisite — especially in this case where the complaint involves the PROMOTER GROUP and potentially implicates management. The Audit Committee can directly engage external investigators or handle the matter independently. Routing such a serious complaint through the CFO's team would compromise independence and potentially expose the whistleblower. Options A, B, and D are all CORRECT statements about the vigil mechanism: (A) Audit Committee oversight and whistleblower protection are mandated; (B) confidentiality of the whistleblower's identity is required; (D) direct access to the Audit Committee chairperson is a mandatory feature. The scenario deliberately mentions that the complaint involves the PROMOTER GROUP to test whether students understand that complaints against senior management/promoters must go directly to the Audit Committee (or its chairperson), not through the regular management chain.

questions.question: DVTL is ranked 180th by market capitalisation, making it one of the top 250 listed entities. Which of the following governance requirements applies SPECIFICALLY to top 250 entities but NOT to all listed entities, and is DVTL currently non-compliant with based on the facts in the scenario?

options.A: The chairperson must be a non-executive director, and the chairperson and the MD must not be related to each other — DVTL's compliance cannot be assessed from the scenario as the Chairman's details are not fully provided
options.B: The board must have at least one independent woman director — DVTL already has Ms. Rekha Srinivasan as an independent woman director on the Audit Committee, so this is compliant
options.C: At least half the board must comprise independent directors when the chairperson is executive — with the scenario not specifying whether DVTL's chairperson is executive or non-executive, this cannot be assessed, but the 4 IDs out of 10 board members (40%) would be non-compliant if the chairperson is executive
options.D: The company must constitute a separate Stakeholders Relationship Committee with an independent director as chairperson — DVTL's compliance with this cannot be determined from the scenario

questions.explanation: Option C best addresses the question. For top 250 entities, Regulation 17(1)(b) requires that if the chairperson is an executive director, at least half the board must be IDs. DVTL has 4 IDs out of 10 directors (40%). If the chairperson is executive, this falls short of the 50% (5 IDs) requirement. The scenario mentions the MD (Mr. Nikhil Agarwal) but does not explicitly state whether there is a separate executive chairman. However, Option C correctly identifies this as a potential non-compliance that is specifically applicable to top 250 entities (through Regulation 17's enhanced governance norms). Option A describes Regulation 17(1B) which applies to top 500 entities (not specifically top 250) and is partially relevant — the separation of Chairman/MD roles. Option B describes a requirement for all listed entities (not specific to top 250). Option D describes a requirement under Regulation 20 that applies to all listed entities. The key scenario fact is DVTL's ranking (180th), placing it in the top 250 bracket where stricter governance norms apply. The 4 IDs out of 10 directors detail becomes critical when combined with the top 250 status.
